L88: ###### Definition 2.
L89: 
L90: Let $𝒳$ be a nominal set. Two elements $x,y\in 𝒳$ are nominally equivalent (denoted $x{\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}y$) if $\pi \cdot x=y$ for some $\pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$. Note ${\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}$ is an equivalence relation.
L91: For each $x\in 𝒳$, we define its orbit $𝕆(x)$ to be its ${\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}$-equivalence class; whereas for each finite $N\subseteq 𝔸$ we let ${𝕆}_{N}(x)$ be its $N$-orbit, i.e. its closure under permutations fixing $N$:
L92:  | $𝕆(x)$  | $=\{\pi \cdot x\mid \pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}\}$  | ${𝕆}_{N}(x)$  | $=\{\pi \cdot x\mid \forall a\in N.\pi (a)=a\}$  |
L93: 
L94: Observe that $𝕆(x)={𝕆}_{\mathrm{\varnothing }}(x)$. Moreover, for any $S\subseteq 𝒳$ with finite support we let:
L95: 
L96:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L97: 
L98: the closure of $S$ be $𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(S)=\{\pi \cdot x\mid x\in S\wedge \pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}\}$;
L99: 
L100:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L101: 
L102: the set of orbits of $S$ be $𝒪(S)=\{{𝕆}_{\mathrm{supp}(S)}(x)\mid x\in S\}$.
L103: We say that a nominal set $𝒳$ is orbit-finite if $𝒪(𝒳)$ is finite. If $𝒳$ is orbit-finite, we let its register index be ${r}_{i}(𝒳)=\mathrm{max}\{|\mathrm{supp}(x)|\mid x\in 𝒳\}$.
L104: Note in particular that $𝕆(x)=𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(\{x\})$, for any $x\in 𝒳$, and $𝒪(𝒳)=\{𝕆(x)\mid x\in 𝒳\}$. Given $N\subseteq {N}^{\prime }$ and any $x\in 𝒳$, we have ${𝕆}_{{N}^{\prime }}(x)\subseteq {𝕆}_{N}(x)\subseteq 𝒳$ and $\mathrm{supp}({𝕆}_{N}(x))\subseteq N$. Moreover, for any finitely supported $S\subseteq 𝒳$ we can see by inspection that:
L105: 
L106:  | $$\bigcup 𝒪(S)=S\subseteq 𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(S)\subseteq 𝒳$$  |
L107: and $\mathrm{supp}(𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(S))=\mathrm{\varnothing }$. Orbit-finiteness essentially captures the notion of a set being “finite up to permutation”, and it is central in the development of automata over nominal sets [【14†5】]. Some useful albeit more technical properties follow.
L108: ###### Lemma 3.
L109: 
L110: Let $𝒳,𝒴$ be nominal sets and $X,Y\subseteq 𝒳$. Then:
L111: 
L112:   1. 1.
L113: 
L114: $\{𝕆(x)\mid x\in X\}=𝒪(𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(X))$ and $|𝒪(𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(X))|\le |𝒪(X)|$;
L115: 
L116:   2. 2.
L117: 
L118: if $X$ has empty support then $𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(X\times Y)=X\times 𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(Y)$;
L119: 
L120:   3. 3.
L121: if $𝒳,𝒴$ are orbit-finite then $|𝒪(𝒳\times 𝒴)|\le |𝒪(𝒳)|\cdot |𝒪(𝒴)|\cdot n_{1}^{}{}_{}{}^{{n}_{2}}\cdot (1+ϵ)$ where $\{{n}_{1},{n}_{2}\}=\{{r}_{i}(𝒳),{r}_{i}(𝒴)\}\ne \{0\}$ and ${n}_{1}\ge {n}_{2}$, and $ϵ\le 1$ is a constant that vanishes for ${n}_{2}\ge 4$.
L122: We next define nominal labelled transition systems, where states and labels form nominal sets, which retain a possibly unbounded history component but are otherwise orbit-finite. For that purpose, orbit-finiteness is relaxed to accommodate histories of unbounded size. One part of our solution is to use configurations comprising pairs of a state $s$ and a history $H$, with $\mathrm{supp}(s)\subseteq H$, where only the set of states is orbit-finite.
L123: The other part is to stipulate that the names appearing only in the history component of a configuration do not matter, in the following way. If a transition can be taken from a given configuration then:
L124:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L125: 
L126: weakening the configuration with some fresh name (i.e. fresh both for the source and target configurations), or
L127: 
L128:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L129: 
L130: strengthening the configuration by removing a name appearing only in its history (and not in its state),
L131: should not affect whether the transition can be taken or not. Note here the asymmetry in the freshness requirements for $a$ in weakening and strengthening: weakening requires that the name be completely fresh. This is in order to account for transitions performing fresh name generation. A transition freshly generating some name $a$ would be rendered invalid if we added $a$ to that transition’s initial history.
L132: ###### Definition 4.
L133: 
L134: A Fresh Nominal Labelled-Transition System (FLTS) is a tuple $ℒ=⟨𝒮,L,\to ⟩$, where (writing ${𝒫}_{\mathrm{fin}}$ for the finite powerset operator):
L135: 
L136:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L137: 
L138: $𝒮$ is a nominal set of states and $L$ is a nominal set of actions,
L139: 
L140:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L141: 
L142: $\to \subseteq \widehat{𝒮}\times L\times \widehat{𝒮}$ is an equivariant transition relation,
L143: 
L144:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L145: where $\widehat{𝒮}=\{(s,H)\in 𝒮\times {𝒫}_{\mathrm{fin}}(𝔸)\mid \mathrm{supp}(s)\subseteq H\}$ is the nominal set of configurations;
L146: 
L147: and such that, for all $(s,H)\stackrel{\ell }{\to }({s}^{\prime },{H}^{\prime })$ and $a\in 𝔸$:
L148: 
L149:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L150: 
L151: $\mathrm{supp}({s}^{\prime })\subseteq \mathrm{supp}(s)\cup \mathrm{supp}(\mathrm{\ell })$ and ${H}^{\prime }=H\cup \mathrm{supp}(\mathrm{\ell })$;
L152: 
L153:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L154: if $a\notin {H}^{\prime }$ then $(s,H\cup \{a\})\stackrel{\ell }{\to }({s}^{\prime },{H}^{\prime }\cup \{a\})$ (weakening);
L155: 
L156:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L157: 
L158: if $a\notin \mathrm{supp}(s)$ then $(s,H\setminus \{a\})\stackrel{\ell }{\to }({s}^{\prime },{H}^{\prime \prime })$ for some ${H}^{\prime \prime }$ (strengthening).
L159: 
L160: $ℒ$ is called fresh-orbit-finite if $𝒮$ and $L$ are orbit-finite.
L161: The notion of FLTS is fairly general and encompasses popular computational scenarios such as name-carrying processes (e.g. in the $\pi $-calculus) and name-manipulating programs (e.g. Java programs with objects). At the automata level, one such formalism is that of fresh-register automata [【19†44】], which are the baseline paradigm in our study. As we are interested in behavioural properties, rather than language acceptance, we disregard initial and final states.
L162: The automata we define next operate on inputs $(t,a)\in \mathrm{\Sigma }\times 𝔸$ where $t$ comes from a finite set of tags and $a$ is a name.
L163: ###### Definition 5.
L164: 
L165: An $r$-Fresh-Register Automaton ($r$-FRA) is a tuple $𝒜=⟨Q,\mu ,\mathrm{\Sigma },\delta ⟩$, where $r\in \mathbb{N}$ is the number of registers in $𝒜$ and:
L166: 
L167:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L168: 
L169: $Q$ is a finite set of states, and $\mu :Q\to 𝒫([1,r])$ an availability function;
L170: 
L171:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L172: 
L173: $\mathrm{\Sigma }$ is a finite set of tags, and $\delta :Q\times \mathrm{\Sigma }\times \{i,{i}^{\bullet },{i}^{⊛}\mid 1\le i\le r\}\times Q$ is the transition relation;
L174: 
L175: subject to the following conditions:
L176:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L177: 
L178: if $(q,t,i,{q}^{\prime })\in \delta $ then $i\in \mu (q)$ and $\mu ({q}^{\prime })\subseteq \mu (q)$;
L179: 
L180:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L181: 
L182: if $(q,t,{i}^{\bullet },{q}^{\prime })\in \delta $ or $(q,t,{i}^{⊛},{q}^{\prime })\in \delta $, then $\mu ({q}^{\prime })\subseteq \mu (q)\cup \{i\}$.
L183: 
L184: We shall write $q\stackrel{t,x}{\to }{q}^{\prime }$ for $(q,t,x,{q}^{\prime })\in \delta $.
L185: We can see that the labels appearing in FRA transitions are of the form $(t,x)$, where $t$ comes from a finite alphabet while $x$ is a variant of a register index $i$. In fact, the approaches are incomparable: fresh-orbit-finite LTSs (where model checking is decidable) are more general than the orbit-finite LTSs of [【36†15】], but our logic is less general than theirs. Using $\mathrm{\#}u$, we can define fresh quantification:

L351:

L529: We proceed to showing the correspondence between the semantics of an $\mu $FHML formula and its corresponding parity game.
L530: ###### Theorem 30.
L531: 
L532: Given a $\mu $FHML formula ${\varphi }_{0}$, $𝒰$-variable assignment $\xi $, FLTS $ℒ$ and $({s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ from $ℒ$, we have $({s}_{0},{H}_{0})\in {⟦{\varphi }_{0}⟧}_{\xi }$ iff Defender wins from $({s}_{0},{H}_{0},\xi ,{\varphi }_{0})$ in $𝒢(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},\xi ,{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$.
L533: We have thus reduced model checking of formulas to winning in parity games. At this stage, we can restrict our attention to closed (firm negation-free) formulas ${\varphi }_{0}$. The next step is deciding winning regions of our parity games. The latter requires the games to be finite, whereas ours are not so. We therefore reduce our parity games to equivalent finite ones. For this to be possible, we restrict our attention to FLTSs that are fresh-orbit-finite.
L534: For brevity, in the remainder of this section we shall say that $(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ is a setup of grade $\mathrm{N}$ if:
L535: 
L536:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L537: 
L538: $ℒ$ is a fresh-orbit-finite FLTS with set of states $𝒮$, and $({s}_{0},{H}_{0})\in \widehat{𝒮}$;
L539: 
L540:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L541: 
L542: ${\varphi }_{0}$ is a closed (firm negation-free) $\mu $FHML formula;
L543: 
L544:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L545: 
L546: $N=|\mathrm{supp}({\varphi }_{0})|+\Vert {\varphi }_{0}\Vert +{r}_{i}(𝒮)$.
L547: Given a setup $(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ of grade $N$, we first present a version of $𝒢(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ with bounded histories. The idea is to restrict the size of the history to the maximum number of names that are available to the formula and the states of the FLTS, and one extra to represent a fresh name. This amounts to a bound of $N+1$ names.
L548: When a new name is added and the size of the history is greater than $N$, then names that are in the history but no longer present in the formula are forgotten. Each position in this game is a tuple $(s,H,\varphi )$ with $|H|\le N+1$.
L549: ###### Definition 31.
L550: 
L551: Let $(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ be a setup of grade $N$. The history-bounded game ${𝒢}_{N}(ℒ,{\varphi }_{0},{s}_{0},{H}_{0})$ has root position $({s}_{0},{H}_{0}^{\prime },{\varphi }_{0})$, for some ${H}_{0}^{\prime }{⊲}_{N}({s}_{0},{\varphi }_{0},{H}_{0})$, and game rules as in 【63†Definition 27】, apart from the rule for modal connectives:
